title: HelioDocs x Redwood — POC scoping (mixed long-context summarization + chat p95)
summary: POC scoping call focused on HelioDocs’ requirement to maintain strong p95 latency for interactive chat while running long-context (8k–32k) summarization jobs on the same capacity. Customer asked for “p95 guarantees” and for proof via benchmark results that reflect their mixed prompt-length distribution. Redwood proposed running the mixed-workload benchmark suite (trace-like replay + synthetic distributions) on a Dedicated SKU and sharing p50/p95/p99 plus queueing metrics (wait time, prefill vs decode split). Discussed scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware dispatch under feature flag) as a mitigation for tail spikes observed under FIFO/co-batching, plus rollout/rollback criteria and what Redwood can/can’t contractually guarantee (SLA vs workload-dependent p95).
topics: POC scope and success criteria; workload characterization (summarization vs chat); p95/p99 definitions and measurement; Dedicated vs Hosted; mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware); benchmarking plan and artifacts; security/data retention questions; timeline and next steps.
next_steps: HelioDocs to send a prompt-length histogram (or anonymized trace stats) for chat + summarization and target SLO definitions (TTFT vs end-to-end).
Redwood (Rina) to run mixed-workload benchmark scenarios using HelioDocs-like distributions and share a results table (baseline vs scheduler flag on).
Redwood (Omar) to confirm instrumentation: per-class queue depth, wait time histograms, and prefill/decode split, and provide a short readout of what will be monitored during POC.
Redwood (Lauren) to send Dedicated POC proposal: capacity sizing assumptions, region, security posture (data retention/logging), and pricing/contracting notes about latency targets.
Schedule follow-up review of benchmark results and POC plan (60 min).
action_items: HelioDocs (Priya Nair) — Provide workload details: context length distribution, concurrency targets, token-out ranges, and whether chat is streaming. Due: 2024-11-08
HelioDocs (Jordan Lee) — Confirm deployment constraints: VPC requirement, outbound egress allowlist, and data retention expectations. Due: 2024-11-08

Redwood (Rina Kobayashi) — Run mixed-workload benchmark suite with HelioDocs-like mix (e.g., 70/30 chat vs summarization; 12k–32k contexts) and produce baseline vs prototype tables (p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU util). Due: 2024-11-12
Redwood (Omar El-Sayed) — Share metric definitions + dashboard screenshots: queue wait time, per-class depth, prefill/decode breakdown; propose rollback triggers for POC. Due: 2024-11-11
Redwood (Lauren Bishop) — Send POC scoping email: proposed Dedicated sizing + timeline + what p95 can be targeted under defined workload. Due: 2024-11-08
transcript:
Fireflies.ai
Meeting: HelioDocs x Redwood — POC scoping (mixed long-context summarization + chat p95)
Recorded: 2024-11-06 17:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes

Attendees:
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood Inference)
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood Inference)
- Rina Kobayashi (Redwood Inference)
- Amit Shah (HelioDocs)
- Priya Nair (HelioDocs)
- Jordan Lee (HelioDocs)
- Elena Petrova (HelioDocs)

---

[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Cool, alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is Lauren from Redwood. Omar and Rina are on as well. Um, the goal today is to scope a POC and be really concrete on what success looks like—especially around the mixed workload thing you mentioned: long context summarization plus interactive chat.

[00:18] Amit Shah: Yep, thanks Lauren. That’s exactly it. We’ve had tail latency issues with our current setup. We want to understand if Redwood can give us, like, p95 guarantees even when we’re doing long-context summarization jobs in the background.

[00:31] Lauren Bishop: Got it. When you say “p95 guarantees,” do you mean an SLA in the contract sense, or do you mean you want us to prove—under a defined workload—that the p95 stays under a target?

[00:43] Amit Shah: More the second. Like we need evidence. We can’t go to leadership with “it should be fine.” We need a test plan with numbers.

[00:52] Elena Petrova: And product cares about the chat experience. If a user is chatting and it takes, like, 5 seconds because some batch summarization kicked off, we get killed.

[01:02] Omar El-Sayed: Makes sense. Just to anchor terms—sometimes teams mix up “time to first token” with “end-to-end completion.” For chat, do you care about TTFT p95, or total response latency p95, or both?

[01:15] Priya Nair: Both, but TTFT is the big one. If TTFT is bad it feels broken. And then also overall time can’t explode.

[01:24] Jordan Lee: We stream responses today, so users see tokens right away, ideally.

[01:30] Omar El-Sayed: OK. Streaming helps because we can treat first token separately. But the scheduler in the runtime matters a lot when long prefill requests are in the same queues.

[01:41] Lauren Bishop: Before we dive into Redwood specifics—can you walk us through your workloads? What percent is chat vs summarization? Context sizes? And is summarization running on the same serving fleet today?

[01:53] Priya Nair: Roughly, chat is the majority of interactive traffic, like 60–80%. Summarization is maybe 20–40% depending on the day. The summarization is heavy—long contexts, 8k up to 32k tokens. Sometimes more, but we cap.

[02:09] Priya Nair: Chat contexts are shorter, like 1k to 4k typical, but occasionally a user has long thread history.

[02:17] Jordan Lee: And yeah, it’s the same GPU pool. That’s partly because we don’t want to dedicate separate infra; we want to keep utilization up.

[02:25] Amit Shah: But the tradeoff is tail latency. Our p95 jumps when the summarization jobs ramp.

[02:31] Omar El-Sayed: Right. Long context is prefill-heavy. Those requests sit on the GPU for a while before you even get the first token out. If you have FIFO dispatch, the chat requests can end up waiting behind one or more long prefill batches.

[02:45] Lauren Bishop: Do you have a concrete target? Like “TTFT p95 under X ms”?

[02:51] Elena Petrova: We want TTFT p95 under 800 milliseconds for chat, and ideally under 500. End-to-end for a typical response, maybe p95 under 3 seconds, but that depends on tokens.

[03:04] Amit Shah: And we want it consistent. Not like it’s OK until a batch job starts and then it’s 2–4 seconds.

[03:12] Lauren Bishop: Got it. And on summarization, are you okay with it being slower as long as it doesn’t crush chat?

[03:18] Priya Nair: Yes. Summarization is async. We can tolerate higher latency there. Just don’t starve it entirely.

[03:25] Omar El-Sayed: That’s the core scheduling tradeoff: protect short/interactive latency without starving long requests.

[03:31] Lauren Bishop: OK. Are you currently on a hosted API or dedicated GPUs with someone else? Or self-hosted?

[03:36] Jordan Lee: We have a mix. We tried AWS Bedrock for some things, OpenAI for others. But for long context we’ve also tried a self-hosted vLLM cluster because costs.

[03:48] Amit Shah: Together AI was in the mix too, but we still see tail spikes when we co-locate jobs.

[03:54] Lauren Bishop: Understood.

[03:56] Rina Kobayashi: One quick clarifying thing: when you say p95, are you measuring at the client, like wall-clock including network, or at the server? Because POC results differ.

[04:06] Priya Nair: Client side in prod. For POC, we can accept server-side as long as it’s apples to apples and you provide enough detail.

[04:14] Omar El-Sayed: We can provide both: server-side latency breakdown (queue wait vs service time; and prefill vs decode) plus client-observed numbers if you run from your VPC or a known region.

[04:27] Lauren Bishop: Let me outline what we can do for a POC. We can run a mixed-workload benchmark suite that simulates your distribution—short chat prompts and long summarization prompts arriving concurrently. We measure p50/p95/p99, plus throughput, GPU utilization, and queueing metrics.

[04:45] Lauren Bishop: And we can run two configurations: baseline scheduler and our prototype mixed-workload scheduler behind a flag.

[04:54] Amit Shah: Prototype? That sounds risky.

[04:57] Omar El-Sayed: It’s not default-on yet, but it’s exactly aimed at this problem. It classifies requests as “short” vs “long” based on prompt length and predicted prefill cost, then uses a two-queue policy. Short requests get priority for dispatch, and we add fairness bounds so long requests still make progress.

[05:18] Priya Nair: Is it strictly length-based? Because sometimes the same length can have different compute.

[05:23] Omar El-Sayed: Today it’s a combination. Prompt length is the primary feature; we also have a predicted prefill cost stub and we’ve been testing using observed prefill time as an EWMA. But for POC we can keep it conservative and transparent. You’ll see the classification thresholds.

[05:41] Jordan Lee: What happens if it misclassifies? Like a request that’s “short” but actually long.

[05:47] Omar El-Sayed: Failure mode is you might let a heavy request into the short queue, which can hurt short p95. That’s why the defaults are conservative, and we also track queue wait time and starvation signals. If we see short queue wait rising, we can tune the threshold.

[06:05] Lauren Bishop: Also, for the POC we can start without the prototype flag and then enable it once we have baseline numbers. We can treat it as an experiment, not a commitment.

[06:15] Amit Shah: OK, but our ask is proof. We need to see that chat p95 doesn’t blow up when summarization is running.

[06:24] Rina Kobayashi: Totally. The way we typically do this: you provide a “traffic model”—even just a histogram of input lengths and output lengths for both workloads, plus concurrency targets. We then run a set of standardized scenarios.

[06:38] Rina Kobayashi: Example: 70% chat at 1–4k context, 30% summarization at 12–32k context, with burst patterns. We capture p95 TTFT and p95 end-to-end for chat, and throughput for summarization.

[06:53] Elena Petrova: Can you simulate bursts? Because the worst case for us is a bunch of summarization jobs start at once.

[06:59] Rina Kobayashi: Yes. We have bursty arrival patterns and also “step function” ramps. We can include a scenario where summarization goes from 0% to 40% over like 2 minutes.

[07:11] Jordan Lee: Do you also track queue depth? Because we want to understand what’s happening when it degrades.

[07:16] Omar El-Sayed: Yes. For the scheduler we expose per-class queue depth, wait time histograms, and we can do tracing spans for enqueue and dequeue events. It’s helpful for explaining p95 changes.

[07:30] Amit Shah: What about dedicated vs hosted? We’re leaning dedicated if it means stable latency.

[07:36] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated is usually the right fit for “stable p95 under mixed workloads” because you avoid noisy neighbors and you can reserve capacity. But note: even on dedicated capacity, if you run both workloads on the same reserved pool, you still need scheduling to keep tails in check.

[07:55] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated gives you isolation from other customers and predictable throughput. Scheduler helps with internal contention.

[08:04] Priya Nair: Makes sense.

[08:06] Jordan Lee: Security-wise, we’ll likely need a VPC deployment eventually, but for POC can we do hosted dedicated in your cloud?

[08:13] Lauren Bishop: We can do Dedicated capacity in our environment with strict isolation and private networking options, and we can talk about VPC peering / private link depending on region. For POC, many customers start with Dedicated in our cloud and restrict logging.

[08:28] Jordan Lee: Data retention is a question. We can’t have prompts stored.

[08:32] Lauren Bishop: By default, we don’t retain prompts for training. Operational logs can be configured—like metadata only, or sampled structured logs. For a POC we can set it to minimal retention. Omar can speak to what’s necessary for debugging.

[08:46] Omar El-Sayed: For performance debugging we don’t need full prompt text. We primarily need token counts, timings, request IDs, queue class labels, and maybe route/model version.

[08:58] Priya Nair: Good.

[09:01] Amit Shah: Can we go back to “guarantees”? I know you can’t sign “p95 under 800ms no matter what,” but we need a statement we can rely on.

[09:11] Lauren Bishop: Right. What we typically do is define a workload envelope for the POC and for production—like max context length, max concurrency, prompt mix, and target region. We can then commit to an SLA for uptime/availability and provide guidance plus monitoring/alerting to stay inside the envelope. The benchmark results become the proof point.

[09:34] Elena Petrova: So the guarantee is conditional.

[09:36] Lauren Bishop: Exactly. Latency is always workload-dependent.

[09:40] Rina Kobayashi: In the benchmark report we can be explicit: “Under scenario A with X distribution and Y RPS, TTFT p95 is Z.”

[09:50] Amit Shah: OK.

[09:52] Priya Nair: What models are we talking about? We use a mix of Llama variants.

[09:56] Lauren Bishop: We can align on the model you want in the POC. If you’re on an open model like Llama 3.x or something similar, we can test that directly. The scheduler behavior is mostly model-agnostic, but the prefill cost depends on architecture and KV cache behavior.

[10:14] Priya Nair: We’re considering a 70B class model for summarization, smaller for chat.

[10:20] Omar El-Sayed: If they’re different models, the scheduling problem changes a bit. Are they sharing the same runtime instance? Or would you run separate deployments?

[10:28] Jordan Lee: Today, we run them in the same cluster but different endpoints. It still contends on GPU if we pack.

[10:36] Omar El-Sayed: Right. If it’s the same GPU pool and we do smart routing and admission control, we can still handle it. But we should define whether the POC is “single model mixed prompts” or “two endpoints sharing capacity.”

[10:52] Amit Shah: Good point. For POC, we can simplify: assume one model. If that works, we can extend.

[11:00] Lauren Bishop: That’s usually best.

[11:02] Rina Kobayashi: For the mixed-workload benchmark suite we can also run a two-route scenario, but it’s extra plumbing. Let’s start with one model.

[11:14] Priya Nair: OK.

[11:16] Lauren Bishop: Let’s capture your key success criteria. I heard: chat TTFT p95 under 800ms under mixed load, and no big p99 spikes. Anything else?

[11:27] Elena Petrova: Also consistency over time. Like you don’t want oscillation—good then bad.

[11:33] Omar El-Sayed: We can add a stability metric: queue depth should not monotonically grow, and we can look for oscillations during bursts.

[11:41] Jordan Lee: Throughput for summarization: we don’t want it to be 10x slower.

[11:46] Priya Nair: Yeah. If chat gets protected but summarization never finishes, that’s not acceptable.

[11:53] Omar El-Sayed: The scheduler has fairness bounds. One pattern is: serve N short requests then force a long dispatch if long queue wait exceeds a threshold.

[12:06] Priya Nair: Is it configurable?

[12:08] Omar El-Sayed: Yes, weights and fairness window can be tuned under a feature flag. For POC we’ll keep it simple.

[12:18] Lauren Bishop: Rina, can you describe what you’ll deliver as a benchmark artifact?

[12:23] Rina Kobayashi: Sure. We typically produce a table per scenario: baseline vs policy-on. Columns: p50/p95/p99 TTFT and end-to-end for chat, throughput tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and queue wait time p95. We can also include plots for tail distributions.

[12:43] Rina Kobayashi: And we annotate any regressions, like if throughput drops more than, say, 5–10%.

[12:50] Amit Shah: We’d like the raw data too, not just a screenshot.

[12:54] Rina Kobayashi: Yep, we can share CSV-style outputs.

[12:58] Jordan Lee: What hardware would you test on? Because that matters.

[13:02] Lauren Bishop: We can propose a Dedicated SKU—like H100s or A100s depending on your cost envelope. If you tell us your target spend and throughput, we can pick. For tail latency, H100 is usually better, but not always required.

[13:17] Amit Shah: We’re open, but cost matters. Our current self-host is A100.

[13:23] Lauren Bishop: OK. We can run on A100 for apples-to-apples.

[13:27] Omar El-Sayed: Also, for long contexts, memory bandwidth and KV cache behavior matter; A100 vs H100 changes the absolute numbers. But the scheduler delta—the p95 improvement—should still be visible.

[13:42] Priya Nair: Do you have any numbers already?

[13:44] Omar El-Sayed: I don’t want to quote random numbers because it depends on your distribution, but in general, prioritizing short requests reduces chat p95 materially under mixed load. There can be a small throughput tradeoff.

[13:58] Amit Shah: Small like 5%? 20%?

[14:01] Omar El-Sayed: Typically we try to keep it within single-digit percent, but again, it depends on how aggressive you are in protecting chat.

[14:10] Elena Petrova: If we lose 10% summarization throughput but fix chat, that’s fine.

[14:14] Priya Nair: Agreed.

[14:16] Lauren Bishop: Great. Now, do you have any existing traces? Even anonymized—just timestamps and token counts.

[14:23] Jordan Lee: We can generate aggregated stats. Traces might be tricky due to privacy. But we can give distributions.

[14:30] Omar El-Sayed: Distribution is enough to start.

[14:33] Rina Kobayashi: The minimum I need is: for chat: input token distribution, output token distribution, concurrency target or RPS, and whether streaming. For summarization: input token distribution, output length, and concurrency. And the mix ratio.

[14:52] Priya Nair: We can do that.

[14:54] Lauren Bishop: Timeline-wise, when do you need to make a decision?

[14:59] Amit Shah: Ideally within this quarter. So like 4–6 weeks.

[15:04] Lauren Bishop: That’s doable. We can run benchmarks next week, do a POC environment the week after, and then do a two-week evaluation.

[15:15] Jordan Lee: What does “POC environment” mean? A dedicated endpoint we hit?

[15:19] Lauren Bishop: Yep. Dedicated capacity allocated to you, you get an endpoint and credentials. We can set up network restrictions. And we’ll have dashboards for latency and queueing metrics.

[15:34] Omar El-Sayed: During POC we’ll want to watch: chat TTFT p95, queue depth, and any starvation signals for long queue. If anything goes wrong we can flip the scheduler flag off.

[15:47] Amit Shah: That rollback is immediate?

[15:49] Omar El-Sayed: It’s a config change. Usually minutes. We’d also have a canary approach in production, but for POC it’s simpler.

[15:59] Priya Nair: OK.

[16:01] Elena Petrova: Can you explain what you mean by “starvation signals” in plain terms?

[16:06] Omar El-Sayed: Sure. If we keep prioritizing short requests, the long requests might sit in queue too long. So we track max wait time for long queue and ensure it doesn’t exceed a bound. If it does, we force service for long queue or adjust weights.

[16:23] Elena Petrova: Great.

[16:25] Jordan Lee: Another question—does batching interact with this? Because we’ve seen weird things where short requests get stuck behind a big batch.

[16:32] Omar El-Sayed: Yes. That’s actually one of the pathologies. If you form a prefill batch for long prompts and then a short request arrives, naive systems can’t interrupt. Our scheduling policy tries to avoid priority inversion by controlling how we build batches per class and by admission control thresholds.

[16:53] Priya Nair: Admission control meaning you reject?

[16:56] Omar El-Sayed: It can mean applying backpressure. Not necessarily reject, but limit how many long requests can be in-flight so they don’t inflate the queue for short. It depends on configuration.

[17:10] Amit Shah: We can tolerate some backpressure on summarization.

[17:13] Lauren Bishop: OK.

[17:15] Rina Kobayashi: For the benchmark, we can explicitly model that: summarization arrivals can be capped so chat stays stable.

[17:23] Jordan Lee: That’s what we want.

[17:26] Lauren Bishop: Let’s do a quick round on constraints. Region? Data residency?

[17:31] Jordan Lee: US only for now.

[17:33] Amit Shah: SOC2 is required.

[17:35] Lauren Bishop: Redwood is SOC 2. For POC we can share the report under NDA if needed. Also SSO/SAML—probably later phase, but we support it.

[17:46] Jordan Lee: Great.

[17:48] Priya Nair: Will the POC include embeddings or rerank? Not needed now.

[17:52] Lauren Bishop: We can keep it to chat/generation.

[17:55] Elena Petrova: Also, can you provide “p95 by time of day” or something? We have daily peaks.

[18:01] Omar El-Sayed: In POC we can simulate peaks with bursts, and in the live environment you’ll see time series. We can configure dashboards to show p95 and p99 over time and correlate with queue depth.

[18:16] Rina Kobayashi: And in the benchmark, we include warmup. People often accidentally measure cold-start effects.

[18:21] Priya Nair: Thank you. We’ve been burned by that.

[18:25] Lauren Bishop: OK. I want to make sure we answer the core ask: you want proof that under long-context summarization plus chat, chat p95 stays under target. The deliverable is the benchmark report and then POC telemetry.

[18:42] Amit Shah: Yes.

[18:44] Lauren Bishop: Great. What should we use as initial scenario? 70/30 mix?

[18:49] Priya Nair: Start with 70 chat / 30 summarization. Then test a stress scenario 50/50 maybe.

[18:56] Jordan Lee: And include a burst where summarization goes from 10% to 40% quickly.

[19:02] Rina Kobayashi: OK, I’ll define three scenarios: nominal 70/30, stress 50/50, and burst ramp.

[19:10] Omar El-Sayed: For classification thresholds, we’ll need a split point. For example: “short” is <= 4k prompt tokens and “long” is >= 8k, with a gray zone. We can tune based on your distributions.

[19:25] Priya Nair: For us, chat can sometimes be 6k. But most is under 4k.

[19:30] Omar El-Sayed: We can treat 6k as medium, but for the initial pass, let’s not overfit.

[19:37] Amit Shah: One more thing—some of our chat requests are tool calls, like structured outputs. Does that change scheduling?

[19:43] Omar El-Sayed: Not much at the scheduler level; it changes output length distributions. But tool calls can be shorter completion; that actually helps.

[19:52] Elena Petrova: OK.

[19:54] Lauren Bishop: Any concerns about running this on Dedicated? Like procurement process?

[19:58] Amit Shah: We can do a short-term POC agreement. Procurement will ask about data retention and security docs.

[20:06] Lauren Bishop: I’ll send a scoping email with what we log, retention, and how rollback works.

[20:12] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[20:14] (crosstalk)

[20:15] Priya Nair: Sorry, go ahead.

[20:16] Jordan Lee: No you.

[20:18] Priya Nair: I was going to ask: can you share any evidence from other customers?

[20:23] Lauren Bishop: We can share anonymized learnings, but for your decision we should generate your own numbers. Also, we do have support tickets that look like your issue—tail spikes during long prompt windows. That’s exactly why we’re investing in mixed-workload scheduling.

[20:40] Amit Shah: OK.

[20:42] Rina Kobayashi: For the benchmark run, do you need a specific model? If you tell me, I’ll align the harness.

[20:48] Priya Nair: Let’s use Llama 3.1 70B instruct, if you have it.

[20:52] Lauren Bishop: We can check the catalog; if not, we can use a close equivalent. But likely yes.

[20:58] Omar El-Sayed: And we’ll fix the decoding params to something stable—temperature, top_p—so results aren’t noisy.

[21:06] Priya Nair: Great.

[21:08] Jordan Lee: What about context window? We need 32k.

[21:11] Omar El-Sayed: Yep, we can configure for 32k. That will stress KV cache.

[21:16] Amit Shah: OK.

[21:18] Lauren Bishop: Let’s talk about how you’ll evaluate during POC. Will you replay traffic? Or run synthetic tests?

[21:25] Jordan Lee: Synthetic plus a subset of real prompts if legal approves. But likely synthetic.

[21:31] Omar El-Sayed: If synthetic, just make sure token lengths match reality. The scheduler cares mostly about lengths and arrival patterns.

[21:39] Priya Nair: That’s manageable.

[21:42] Lauren Bishop: Great. I think we’re aligned.

[21:45] Rina Kobayashi: I’ll summarize what I need from you. Priya, can you send me distributions by Friday? Input length histograms and target RPS/concurrency for each class.

[21:55] Priya Nair: Yes.

[21:57] Rina Kobayashi: Jordan, if you can confirm whether you want streaming on chat tests and what your measurement point is.

[22:03] Jordan Lee: Yes, streaming on. Measurement at client, but we’ll accept server metrics too.

[22:09] Rina Kobayashi: OK.

[22:11] Lauren Bishop: Omar, anything else we should call out around rollbacks?

[22:14] Omar El-Sayed: For POC, we’ll define rollback triggers like: chat TTFT p95 increases by more than, say, 20% from baseline for 10 minutes, or queue depth keeps growing. We can also set alerts on long queue max wait to avoid starvation.

[22:31] Amit Shah: That’s exactly the type of rigor we want.

[22:34] Elena Petrova: Can we get those triggers in writing?

[22:37] Lauren Bishop: Yes, in the scoping email.

[22:40] --- (Transcript continues; minor transcription gaps) ---

[22:41] Speaker 1: One question about pricing.

[22:43] Lauren Bishop: Yeah.

[22:44] Amit Shah: For POC, do we pay for dedicated capacity?

[22:47] Lauren Bishop: Typically yes, but we can structure it as a short commit that rolls into production if you proceed. I’ll send options.

[22:56] Amit Shah: OK.

[22:58] Priya Nair: And if the prototype scheduler is required for success, is that something we can keep?

[23:04] Omar El-Sayed: It’s feature-flagged. For a limited set of customers we can enable it with monitoring. Longer term the goal is to graduate it to broader availability once it’s proven.

[23:15] Lauren Bishop: For POC we can absolutely run it. Production rollout would be a staged canary with explicit rollback criteria.

[23:24] Jordan Lee: Good.

[23:26] Elena Petrova: Will we see dashboards in your console or do we need to ingest metrics ourselves?

[23:32] Omar El-Sayed: You’ll see it in Redwood Console. We can also export metrics if needed, but for POC console is easiest.

[23:40] Priya Nair: OK.

[23:42] Lauren Bishop: Alright, I think we can wrap. I’ll recap next steps at the end.

[23:48] (brief pause)

[23:50] Lauren Bishop: Next steps: Priya and Jordan will send workload distributions and constraints by Friday. Rina will run the mixed-workload benchmark suite—baseline and scheduler-flag-on—and share the results table early next week. Omar will send metric definitions and proposed rollback triggers. I’ll send a POC scoping email with Dedicated sizing options, security/logging posture, and timeline. Then we schedule a review meeting to go through the benchmark readout.

[24:14] Amit Shah: Sounds good.

[24:16] Priya Nair: Thanks.

[24:17] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone.

[24:19] Elena Petrova: Thank you.

[24:20] Lauren Bishop: Great, talk soon.

- Customer emphasized p95 TTFT for chat as primary success metric under mixed load.
- Redwood proposed running a mixed-workload benchmark suite and optionally enabling a feature-flagged short/long prompt-aware scheduler during POC.
- POC artifacts to include: p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU utilization, queue wait time histograms, and prefill/decode breakdown.
